html:
The Timucua were a Native American people of northeast and north central Florida and southeast Georgia. They were the largest Indigenous group in that area, made up of about 35 chiefdoms speaking dialects of the Timucua language. At contact they may have numbered as many as 200,000, though estimates vary.

They farmed maize, beans and squash, fished the rivers and coast, and hunted. Chiefdoms such as the Saturiwa, at the mouth of the St. Johns River, and the Utina, further west, were often at war. The name Timucua came from the Saturiwa word for the Utina.

Europeans came early. Hernando de Soto marched through their lands in 1539. The French built Fort Caroline in Saturiwa country in 1564, and drawings made there are among the first European pictures of North American peoples. The Spanish destroyed it in 1565 and founded St. Augustine.

Over the next century Franciscan missions spread among the Timucua in Spanish Florida. Epidemics, labour demands and a failed revolt in 1656 thinned them, and raids by English Carolina and its Creek allies after 1702 destroyed the missions. When Spain handed Florida to Britain in 1763, the last few Timucua left for Cuba. Their southern neighbours were the Calusa.
